title: Forex exec in Romualdez case eyed as state witness
summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has asked the Sandiganbayan to allow the removal of foreign exchange executive Felicito Guevarra from the list of accused in the plunder case against former House speaker…

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has asked the Sandiganbayan to allow the removal of foreign exchange executive Felicito Guevarra from the list of accused in the plunder case against former House speaker Martin Romualdez.

In an omnibus motion, ombudsman prosecutors also asked the Sandiganbayan Third Division to allow Guevarra to testify on the last hearing day on Dec. 4 on Romualdez’s petition for bail as well as to remain in the custody of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI). Plunder is a non-bailable offense.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division disclosed receiving the prosecutors’ motion at yesterday’s bail hearing.
Ombudsman prosecutors requested that Guevarra replace former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) chief Manuel Bonoan as witness at the Dec. 4 bail hearing.
They also manifested their intention to withdraw their motion to have Guevarra’s passport canceled.

Aside from Guevarra, who is president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp., Romualdez’s co-accused are his former personal staff Joselyn Serenio and fugitive former congressman Zaldy Co. The case stemmed from Romualdez’s P7.4-billion alleged kickbacks from flood control projects.
After surrendering to the NBI over the weekend, Guevarra was given by the ombudsman conditional immunity from prosecution.

Deputy Special Prosecutor Omar Sagadal also revealed at yesterday’s hearing Guevarra’s restitution or returning of P343 million, representing his “share in his income from transactions with Romualdez through Serenio.”

Guevarra’s surrender to authorities, as well as his “willingness to come forward and divulge everything,” was “something we did not foresee and it happened so fast that is why we filed our motion,” according to Sagadal.

He added it would also be better to let Guevarra remain in NBI detention, instead of transferring him to the custody of the Bureau of Jail Management of Penology in view of allegations – already debunked – of visitors being let inside the New Quezon City Jail Male Dormitory to accompany Romualdez. Such setup would “put unnecessary risk” to Guevarra, the prosecutor said.
Sagadal also argued Guevarra substituting for Bonoan is compliant with current court rules. Bonoan will remain as a state witness, but not in the bail hearing.

“Our motion for amended information does not change the tune of the prosecution, does not change the allegation and maintains the conspiracy and plunder. All that is being done here is accused Guevarra be dropped as accused, but all are the same,” he said.
The camp of Romualdez through lawyer Rashel Ann Pomoy objected to the ombudsman’s proposal, arguing Guevarra’s supposed statement would be “prejudicial to the defense.”
She maintained that dropping Guevarra as accused “cannot be done through amendment of information” since Romualdez has pleaded not guilty to the plunder case.

Sandiganbayan Associate Justice Karl Miranda, chairman of the Third Division, said the bail hearings have been held “for 30 days” and were “extended” anew since the surrender of Guevarra. Yesterday was supposed to be the last day of the bail hearing.
Miranda also declared that the ombudsman’s motion involving Guevarra has been “submitted for resolution,” hence the uncertainty over whether he or Bonoan would be presented.
The court has scheduled for Nov. 27 the arraignment of Guevarra.

Prior to tackling the motion involving Guevarra, the prosecution presented lawyer Mark David Vergara, member of the ombudsman’s special panel of investigators that prepared the plunder case against Romualdez and the others.

According to Vergara, the ombudsman filed the P7.4-billion plunder case – lower than the P56 billion initially alleged against Romualdez and the others – based on sworn statements by 18 former security staff of Co who allegedly delivered cash in suitcases to three properties named under Romualdez’s alleged dummy companies.

Third Division justices, meanwhile, questioned how ombudsman investigators arrived at the alleged P7.4-billion amount linked to Romualdez, as a prosecution witness acknowledged that the figure was based on a computation of what the former security aides were able to recall.

Vergara, on questioning by the court, admitted that while the documents obtained by the investigation panel showed a bigger figure of P56 billion, the information only alleged P7.4 billion going by what the bodyguards of Co told them.
“I think the basis for the P7.4 billion was the testimonies of the Marines when they were able to make direct participation. It was just an estimate,” the witness said.

Vergara explained that the revised amount was based on specific alleged deliveries recalled by the former Marines, involving deliveries reportedly made two to three times weekly over approximately three years.

Pomoy, on cross-examination, got Vergara to acknowledge that he had no personal knowledge of the alleged suitcase deliveries beyond the statements provided by the former Marines, some of whom have already recanted their previous testimonies.
The investigator also confirmed that the characterization of the deliveries as being “for the benefit of accused Romualdez” was a conclusion reached by the ombudsman’s special panel of investigators.
The defense likewise quizzed the witness on how the panel gathered and evaluated the statements used to support the allegations.

Vergara conceded that the special panel of investigators did not personally interview certain individuals whose statements were included in the investigation, including former Marine Orly Guteza and Co.
“Guteza never appeared before the panel. We were looking for him but we did not get an address,” the witness said.
Affidavits from other witnesses, including Gil Navidad and Christopher Esquivel, had been executed before the special panel was constituted or were obtained through the NBI.
The cross-examination also brought up recantations executed by several individuals whose earlier statements had figured in the investigation.
Vergara confirmed that he was aware of recantations involving Guteza, Rosebert Waupan, Bernard Tube, Benny Boluntate and Cecilio Larroder.
The defense pointed out that Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla had previously expressed doubts about the statements from the former Marines and even called them “procured individuals.”

The defense also questioned the panel’s July 1 driving simulation involving Navidad, which was conducted to test the credibility of his account concerning locations where suitcases were allegedly delivered.
Vergara acknowledged that he did not participate in the simulation and had not checked whether Navidad’s phone could establish previous visits to the locations.
The questioning raised issues concerning the independent verification of witness accounts and the extent to which investigators corroborated the alleged deliveries.
Vergara, however, assured the court that the investigation was conducted with integrity and without bias.
